chunks: Ohm's law, conceptually. The question: Conceptually explain ohm's law.
A metal wire is full of free electrons that can move. A voltage pushes them along, but they keep bumping into the atoms of the metal, so they never speed up forever.
They settle at a steady average drift speed. A bigger push means a faster drift and more current, and resistance is how much the material gets in the way.
Picture a marble rolling down a tilted board covered in pegs. It bounces off pegs all the way down, so it travels at a steady average speed instead of accelerating.
Tilt the board twice as steeply and it moves about twice as fast. The tilt is the voltage, the pegs are the atoms, and the marble flow is the current.
Real electrons are far more numerous and the drift is very slow, but the logic is the same.
An electron (accent path) zig-zags between collisions with lattice ions (grey).
Each free flight bends slightly with the field, so although the motion is mostly random, there's a slow net drift.
That drift, times the enormous number of electrons, is the current.
Free electron: an electron in a metal that is not stuck to one atom and can carry current. Electric field: the push on each charge, caused by the voltage across the material.
Collision: a bump between an electron and an atom or impurity that wastes some of its energy. Drift speed: the slow average speed at which electrons move along the wire.
Resistance: how hard the material makes it for electrons to move.
Put 1 volts across a wire and 1 milliamps flows. Put 2 volts across it. The push is twice as big, so the drift speed is twice as big, and 2 milliamps flows.
The extra energy lost in the collisions becomes heat, which is why resistors get warm.
If the wire heats up, its atoms jiggle harder, collisions become more frequent, and the resistance rises. That is the whole idea.
"Voltage is the push, current is the flow, and resistance is how much the material fights it.
A voltage creates an electric field that pushes electrons, but they keep colliding with the atoms in the lattice, so they settle at an average drift speed proportional to the field.
Double the voltage, double the drift speed, double the current. That's why V equals IR is linear.
The collisions are also where the I to the 2R heat comes from, and why a hotter metal has higher resistance."
